meta.title: Who really said "If We Should Have to Leave Our Bleached Bones on These Desert Sands in Vain, Then Beware the Anger of the Legions"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No Roman centurion wrote it. The 'Marcus Flavinius' letter first appears in Jean Lartéguy's 1960 novel Les Centurions, and he later called it a fake.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If We Should Have to Leave Our Bleached Bones on These Desert Sands in Vain, Then Beware the Anger of the Legions'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Roman letter. It first appears as the epigraph of Lartéguy's 1960 novel Les Centurions. Lartéguy later said it was a fabrication passed to him.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known text is the epigraph of Lartéguy’s 1960 novel Les Centurions, framed as a letter from the Roman centurion “Marcus Flavinius.” Lartéguy later disowned it: he wrote that the letter was a fabrication that had been passed to him. The English wording comes from Xan Fielding’s translation, and who actually wrote the text has never been settled.

source.excerpt: … if we should have to leave our bleached bones on these desert sands in vain, then beware of the anger of the Legions!
trail: 1960: The text appears as the epigraph of Jean Lartéguy’s French novel Les Centurions. Quote Investigator calls this the earliest known appearance (Quote Investigator ↗).
1962: Xan Fielding’s English translation, The Centurions (E. P. Dutton), prints the closing line as “then beware of the anger of the Legions!” (Quote Investigator ↗).

1966: Robert Debs Heinl’s Dictionary of Military and Naval Quotations (U.S. Naval Institute) reprints an altered version with no source, ending “beware the anger of the Legions!” (Quote Investigator ↗).
2012: Researcher Garson O’Toole asks the American Dialect Society list whether the letter is fiction. He reports finding no evidence for it earlier than Lartéguy’s novel (ADS-L ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the closing line as Quote Investigator transcribes it from the 1962 English edition. Fielding wrote “beware of the anger.” The shorter “beware the anger of the Legions” matches the version reprinted in the 1966 Dictionary of Military and Naval Quotations.

author.name: Jean Lartéguy
author.heading: About the earliest source
author.bio: Jean Lartéguy was the pen name of Jean Pierre Lucien Osty. He served with the Free French Forces and later became a war correspondent, chiefly for Paris Match. His 1960 novel Les Centurions, about French paratroopers after Indochina, became a bestseller and was filmed as Lost Command (1966). The Marcus Flavinius letter first appears as its epigraph.

Xan Fielding (1962); presented as a letter from a Roman centurion, "Marcus Flavinius," and later disowned by Lartéguy as a fabrication.

misattribution.heading: Who usually gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line usually circulates as a real letter written home by a Roman soldier in the second century. No record of that soldier has been found, and the letter cannot be traced to any source earlier than a French novel published in 1960.

items.why: This is the letter’s stated author. Quote Investigator found no solid historical evidence for the letter or the man and concludes it is a fake whose first known appearance is Lartéguy’s 1960 epigraph (Quote Investigator ↗).
Andrew Bacevich’s June 27, 2010, Washington Post op-ed credited the letter to a Roman commander under this spelling (Quote Investigator ↗).
Later retellings replace “anger” with “fury” or “wrath.” The 1960s text has “anger” (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented source is the epigraph of Jean Lartéguy’s novel Les Centurions (1960). In La Guerre nue (English: The Face of War, 1979) Lartéguy wrote that the letter was a fake, saying it had been fabricated by Roger Frey and reached him through Jean Pouget. Nobody has independently confirmed that account (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: Les Centurions follows French paratroopers from Indochina to the war in Algeria. The “Roman” letter at the front of the book complains that soldiers fighting far from home are betrayed by the politicians behind them, which matches the novel’s theme. Once the text was cut loose from the novel, it began circulating as a genuine ancient document.

It was later used to comment on American wars. A 1969 Cleveland Plain Dealer article tied it to U.S. soldiers in Vietnam, and Andrew Bacevich quoted it in the Washington Post in 2010, according to Quote Investigator ↗.
detailsBody: We can’t say. Lartéguy published the letter first, but later denied writing it. In The Face of War (translated by Beth de Bilio, Bobbs-Merrill, 1979, pp. 291–292) he wrote that it “had been fabricated by Roger Frey,” according to Quote Investigator ↗. That is his own account, and no one has corroborated it, so the page credits the text to Lartéguy as its earliest known publisher without claiming he wrote it.
